verdicts.summary: The CSRF token is tied to the DPoP session id from the load call. If the cached relay token rotates before Approve, the decision fails with 'Enter a pairing code instead' and is never retried.
verdicts.scenario: 1) The owner opens /approve-agent. The load uses the cached token T1 (session S1), and the csrfToken is signed over S1 (McpOAuth.ts:310-319). 2) Before the owner clicks Approve, the cached token passes the refresh threshold (service.ts:398), or renewDpopBeforeExpiry rotates it (service.ts:576-597). That second case is possible because the hosted page builds the full connection layer for saved environments (apps/web/src/connection/runtime.ts:61-67). 3) The decision call gets T2. A renewal is its own session (SessionStore.test.ts:150-160 revokes the original and the renewal separately), so its session id is S2. 4) timingSafeEqualBase64Url fails at McpOAuth.ts:474 and the server refuses. 5) The decision call has no isUnauthorizedResponse retry (connectMcpApproval.ts:99-106). McpConsent only sets errorMessage and never reloads the details (ConnectAgentSurface.tsx:211-220). Whether a renewal always gets a new sessionId comes from the test structure, not from reading the issuance code.
verdicts.consequence: The owner sees 'Your session cannot approve this request. Enter a pairing code instead.' on a page that has no code field. They can only recover by reloading the page.

verdicts.summary: Every step has a time limit. The first authorizeDpopHttp is capped at 30s by the forked exchange's timeout, and the request plus one retry are capped at 10s.
verdicts.scenario: The relay hangs during the token exchange at line 64, which is outside REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS. The forked exchange still times out after 30s with ConnectionTransientError, which mapError turns into ConnectMcpApprovalUnavailableError. With no cloud identity the call fails at once with sessionPending.

verdicts.summary: Both header fields are optionalKey, so `headers: {}` is valid. Every caller (ConnectAgentSurface, PeerLinks, connectMcpApproval) passes headers.
verdicts.scenario: I searched for callers of approval or decision that do not pass headers. There are only four, and all of them pass headers. With `{}` there is no Authorization header, so authenticateRequest uses the cookie, and the PeerLinks pairing-code decision never reads a session.

verdicts.summary: The hazard in this redirect is that a visitor who is not the owner has no code fallback, which finding 0 already reports. The peerLink exclusion and the linkState fallback (orElseSucceed) behave as the note describes.

The server always advertises mcpHostedApproval, and the wizard drops the code whenever it is set. Whether the hosted app at the configured URL (app.t3.codes or nightly.app.t3.codes) actually serves /approve-agent depends on deployment.
verdicts.missing: Deployment state of the hosted app at DEFAULT_HOSTED_APP_URL and NIGHTLY_HOSTED_APP_URL. This repository cannot show it.

verdicts.summary: The client accepts everything the server can register: https, or http on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1].
verdicts.scenario: I tried an http://[::1]:port/cb redirect. URL.hostname is '[::1]', which isLoopbackHost accepts at line 54. A custom scheme such as vscode:// is rejected at registration by parseRedirect, so it never reaches the client.

verdicts.summary: Stale loads are ignored, and the Approve button needs both 'armed' and a ready state. The only failure on the decision path is the CSRF rotation reported under note 0.
verdicts.scenario: React StrictMode mounts twice, so load runs twice. The first effect's cleanup sets cancelled, and its answer is dropped.

verdicts.summary: Every redirectTo the server returns is either a verified registered redirect URI or a redirectWith call on one. Registration allows only https or loopback http, which agentRedirectUrl accepts.
verdicts.scenario: A deny decision or a validation error redirects to error.redirectUri. That value is checked against the client's registered list (McpOAuth.ts:370-377) before any redirect error is built.

verdicts.summary: The open question, whether the server enforces the remote-clients denial for hosted approvals, is finding 4. The fallback page with no code is finding 3. For this machine, the wizard's mcpUrl comes from linkState.tunnelHostname, the same value the server compares against.
The wrapper has the same run-and-squash shape as mintMcpApprovalCodeOn. Every failure comes back as Result.fail, which connectTransport maps to a message.
verdicts.scenario: When the command fails, squashAtomCommandFailure returns the error. isUnavailable then picks the T3 Connect message, and any other error shows the generic 'Could not reach'. Nothing throws out of send.

verdicts.summary: The hosted approval checks the agent's resource and sets `iss` from the origin of the hosted app's own request through the relay, not from the agent's request.
verdicts.scenario: The agent's authorize request carries resource=https://<tunnel>/mcp. The hosted page sends approval and decision to authorized.httpBaseUrl (the relay endpoint). requestUrls takes the issuer from that request's URL (McpOAuth.ts:71-77). If the relay or tunnel forwards a Host header other than the tunnel hostname, sameResource fails (McpOAuth.ts:397-398) and the agent receives invalid_target. If the request passes, the iss in the code redirect would be a different origin. The new test exercises only an in-process handler, never the relay hop.
verdicts.missing: How the relay or Cloudflare tunnel sets the Host header that reaches requestUrl, and whether RelayManagedEndpoint.httpBaseUrl always equals the tunnel hostname. That is relay runtime behaviour, not in this checkout.
